Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- British TV channels could advertise abortion services for the first time under new advertising rules proposed Thursday by an ad industry group. The new proposals will also allow condoms to be advertised more widely on television. The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, the industry body responsible for writing and enforcing advertising rules in Britain, said the commercials would be for pregnancy advisory services that give information about a range of options to pregnant women, including abortion. If an organization does not offer information about abortion, it would have to make that clear in the ad, BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said. Abortion clinics, which require referrals from doctors or hospitals, would not be allowed to advertise under the proposed rules, Taffe said. There would be no restrictions on when such ads could air on British television, she said, but programmers would have to keep the sensitive topic in mind and not schedule the ads around religious programs, for example. "It's a sensitive product, so it would have to be scheduled sensitively," Taffe told CNN. The proposal is among a number of updates to current advertising standards that the Committee for Advertising Practice and BCAP, its broadcasting arm, published Thursday after an 18-month review. "Each year the British public (sees) millions of advertisements, many of which are memorable," the committee said. "The advertising codes aim to make sure that they are memorable for the right reasons." The public now has until June 19 to comment on the proposals before they come into force, likely in 2010, the committee said. The new proposals also contain a change on advertising condoms on television. Under current rules, condoms generally cannot be advertised on TV before 9 p.m. in order to protect younger viewers, the committee said. New rules would relax the restrictions on advertising condoms, with the only requirement that they not be shown around programs intended for children younger than 10. The change came after Joyce Gould, a member of the House of Lords, requested the change and noted that Britain had the highest teenage pregnancy rate in Europe along with spiraling rates of sexually transmitted diseases, the committee said. Gould reported a survey that showed young people believed TV was one of the most effective ways of encouraging them to use condoms. "The presence of condom advertisements on television continues to be a subject of complaint to the (Advertising Standards Authority), but numbers are very low," the committee said. "Nevertheless, BCAP has to balance public sensitivities against a public health problem that is clearly urgent."

The proposals would also allow condoms to be advertised more widely on television.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, the industry body responsible for writing and enforcing advertising rules in Britain, said the commercials would promote pregnancy advisory services that provide information about a range of options for pregnant women, including abortion.

The public has until June 19 to comment on the proposals before they come into force, likely in 2010, the committee said.

The new proposals also include a change to rules governing condom advertising on television. Under current rules, condoms generally cannot be advertised on television before 9 p.m. in order to protect younger viewers, the committee said.

The proposed rules would relax restrictions on condom advertising, requiring only that such ads not be shown around programs intended for children younger than 10.

The proposed changes would also make it easier for condom advertisements to appear on TV.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, the industry body that creates and applies advertising regulations in Britain, said the ads would promote pregnancy advice services offering women information about multiple choices during pregnancy, including abortion.

BCAP spokeswoman Lynsay Taffe said that if a group does not provide information about abortion, it would be required to state that clearly in its advertisement.

Taffe also said that abortion clinics themselves would not be permitted to advertise under the proposed rules, because they require referrals from doctors or hospitals.

According to Taffe, the proposals would not set specific limits on the times such advertisements could be broadcast on British television. However, broadcasters would be expected to treat the issue carefully when scheduling them, avoiding placement near programming such as religious shows.

“It’s a sensitive product, so it would have to be scheduled sensitively,” Taffe told CNN.

The proposal is part of a wider set of revisions to existing advertising rules released Thursday by the Committee of Advertising Practice and BCAP, its broadcast division, following an 18-month review.

“Each year the British public (sees) millions of advertisements, many of which are memorable,” the committee said. “The advertising codes aim to make sure that they are memorable for the right reasons.”

Members of the public have until June 19 to respond to the proposals before they are implemented, probably in 2010, the committee said.

The draft rules also include changes to how condoms may be advertised on television. At present, condom commercials are generally barred from airing before 9 p.m. as a way to shield younger audiences, the committee said.

The revised rules would loosen those limits. The only restriction would be that condom ads could not be shown around programs aimed at children under the age of 10.

The committee said the change followed a request from Joyce Gould, a member of the House of Lords, who pointed out that Britain had Europe’s highest teenage pregnancy rate, along with rapidly rising levels of sexually transmitted diseases.

Gould cited a survey indicating that young people considered television one of the most powerful methods for encouraging condom use.

“The presence of condom advertisements on television continues to be a subject of complaint to the (Advertising Standards Authority), but numbers are very low,” the committee said. “Nevertheless, BCAP has to balance public sensitivities against a public health problem that is clearly urgent.”

British advertising regulators have proposed changes to television advertising rules that would allow pregnancy advisory services offering information about abortion to advertise on British TV for the first time. The proposals follow an 18-month review of the broadcasting advertising code and are intended to reflect changes in society, healthcare access and public expectations around reproductive health information.

Under the proposed rules, organisations that provide pregnancy counselling or advice, including services that discuss abortion as one possible option, would be permitted to run television advertisements. However, the ads would have to make clear what type of service is being offered. For example, viewers would need to be able to tell whether an organisation provides medical referrals, counselling, abortion-related information, or alternatives to abortion. Regulators said this transparency would be necessary to prevent confusion and ensure that people seeking help understand the nature of the service before making contact.

The proposals would also relax existing restrictions on condom advertising. Condom commercials have traditionally faced limits on when and where they can be shown, particularly because of concerns about younger viewers. The revised rules would make it easier for such advertisements to appear on television, while still requiring broadcasters to schedule them sensitively and avoid placing them around programmes aimed primarily at children.

Supporters of the changes argue that the new rules would improve public access to accurate sexual and reproductive health information. They say television remains an important source of public messaging and that responsible advertising could help people make informed decisions, reduce unwanted pregnancies and promote safer sex.

Critics, however, are likely to raise concerns about whether abortion-related services should be promoted through television advertising and whether younger audiences might be exposed to material that some viewers consider inappropriate. Regulators have sought to address those concerns by proposing safeguards on scheduling, content and disclosure.

The proposals are now open for public consultation. Viewers, broadcasters, health organisations, religious groups and other interested parties will be able to submit comments before the rules are finalised. If approved, the changes are expected to come into force in 2010.

Overall, the proposed reforms mark a significant shift in British television advertising policy. They would broaden the range of reproductive health services that can advertise on TV while maintaining rules designed to ensure that sensitive subjects are handled responsibly.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about proposed UK television advertising rules that would allow abortion service ads for the first time and relax restrictions on condom commercials.
counterfactuals.output:
**London (CNN)** — Proposed changes to UK television advertising rules could allow abortion service providers to advertise on television for the first time and make it easier for condom brands to run commercials before the evening watershed.

The proposals, put forward by the body responsible for writing the UK’s broadcast advertising code, would mark a significant shift in how sexual health services are promoted on British television.

Under the current rules, television advertisements for commercial abortion services are not permitted. The proposed changes would allow ads from organizations offering abortion advice or services, provided they meet strict standards around accuracy, sensitivity and public responsibility.

The changes would also relax long-standing restrictions on condom advertising. At present, condom commercials face limits on when they can be broadcast, particularly around programming likely to be watched by children. The revised rules would allow more condom ads to air earlier in the evening, though they would still be barred from appearing in or around programs aimed at young children.

Supporters of the proposals say the changes reflect modern public health priorities and could help ensure viewers have access to factual information about reproductive and sexual health services. They argue that television advertising can play a role in reducing stigma and encouraging safer sex.

Critics, however, are likely to raise concerns about the potential exposure of younger audiences to sensitive subjects and about the way abortion services may be presented in commercial advertising.

Any advertisements permitted under the new rules would still have to comply with broader UK advertising standards, including requirements that they not mislead viewers, cause serious or widespread offense, or exploit vulnerable audiences.

The proposals are expected to be subject to consultation before any final decision is made. If adopted, they would represent the first time abortion service advertisements could appear on UK television.

counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON —** Britain’s broadcast advertising rule-makers have proposed changes that could allow pregnancy advisory services, including those offering information on abortion, to advertise on television and radio, as part of a wider review of standards covering sensitive health and sexual-health messages.

The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice, or BCAP, said the proposals are intended to bring the advertising code into line with changes in law, public policy and audience expectations. The plans also include revised rules for condom advertising, potentially allowing wider scheduling of ads for condoms while maintaining restrictions around programmes aimed at younger children.

Under the proposed changes, pregnancy advisory services would be able to advertise if they make clear whether they refer women for abortion or do not refer for abortion. BCAP said the requirement is designed to ensure viewers and listeners are not misled about the nature of the advice being offered.

Lynsay Taffe, a spokeswoman for BCAP, said the consultation was aimed at ensuring that broadcast advertising rules remain “transparent, proportionate and easy to understand.”

“These are important and sensitive areas, and it is right that the public, broadcasters, advertisers and interested organisations have the opportunity to comment,” Taffe said.

The proposals would also amend rules on condom advertising. BCAP said condom ads would continue to be subject to scheduling restrictions, but the changes could permit them in a wider range of programmes where the likely audience is appropriate. Supporters of liberalising the rules argue that condom advertising can play a role in public-health campaigns aimed at reducing sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies.

BCAP said its public consultation will seek views from health groups, religious organisations, broadcasters, advertisers, parents and members of the public before final decisions are made. Any changes would apply to broadcast advertising regulated under the UK advertising codes.

Taffe said BCAP was not taking a position on abortion or sexual morality, but was reviewing whether the rules properly balance consumer protection, freedom of expression and public-health information.

“The purpose of the code is to make sure advertising is responsible and not misleading,” she said. “Consultation allows us to test whether the proposed rules achieve that balance.”

The consultation is expected to draw strong responses from reproductive-rights organisations, anti-abortion groups and family campaigners, particularly over whether abortion-related information should be promoted in broadcast media. BCAP said all submissions will be considered before revised standards are adopted.

**London, England —** Britain’s advertising industry has proposed a significant loosening of rules governing how sexual health services can be promoted on television and radio, including allowing abortion service providers to advertise more widely and expanding the hours during which condom commercials may be shown.

The proposals follow an 18-month review of the UK’s broadcast advertising code, which sets standards for television and radio commercials. The review was carried out by the bodies responsible for writing and enforcing advertising rules, and is aimed at updating regulations to reflect changes in public attitudes, health policy and the media landscape.

Under the proposed changes, organizations offering abortion services could be permitted to advertise on broadcast media, provided the ads comply with strict rules on taste, responsibility and protection of younger audiences. The move would mark a notable shift in a highly sensitive area of public health advertising.

The review also recommends requiring pregnancy advisory services to make clear whether they do not refer women for abortions, a measure intended to prevent viewers from being misled about the nature of the help being offered.

Rules on condom advertising would also be relaxed. At present, condom commercials are subject to tight scheduling restrictions. The new proposals would allow them to be broadcast more widely, including earlier in the evening, though limits would remain around programs aimed at children or likely to attract large numbers of younger viewers.

Supporters of the changes argue that advertising can play a legitimate role in public health, particularly in encouraging safer sex and ensuring people know where to find accurate reproductive health information.

But the proposals are likely to draw criticism from anti-abortion campaigners and some family groups, who may argue that broadcast advertising risks normalizing abortion services or exposing children to sexual health messages too early.

Advertising regulators say any changes would not mean a free-for-all. Commercials would still be barred from using shock tactics, making misleading medical claims or targeting children. Ads for sexual health products and services would also remain subject to scheduling controls and content standards.

The proposals are expected to go through consultation before any final changes are adopted. If approved, they would represent one of the most substantial updates to British broadcast advertising rules on reproductive and sexual health in years.

**UK ad regulator weighs allowing pregnancy advice service commercials on TV**

*London* — The Broadcast Committee of Advertising Practice has proposed changing UK television advertising rules to allow commercials for pregnancy advisory services, including services that discuss options after conception.

Under the proposal, pregnancy advisory services would be permitted to advertise on broadcast television, but with restrictions intended to prevent misleading claims and undue pressure on viewers. Services that do not refer women directly for abortion would be required to make that clear in their advertisements.

BCAP said the change would bring broadcast rules more closely into line with non-broadcast advertising standards and reflect the range of lawful pregnancy advice services available in the UK.

The proposal would not amount to unrestricted advertising for abortion clinics. Commercials would be limited to promoting advisory services rather than advertising abortion procedures themselves. Providers would also have to comply with broader advertising rules requiring ads to be responsible, accurate and not harmful or offensive.

BCAP also said broadcasters would need to take care over scheduling. Because pregnancy, abortion and related advice can be sensitive subjects, ads could be subject to placement restrictions to avoid inappropriate contexts or audiences, particularly around programmes likely to be watched by children or where the subject matter could cause distress.

The committee has opened the proposal for public consultation, with comments due by **June 19**. After the comment period closes, BCAP will review responses before deciding whether to amend the UK Code of Broadcast Advertising.

counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON, 2010 —** British television viewers could see more condom advertising before the 9 p.m. watershed under proposed changes to broadcast advertising rules aimed at supporting public health campaigns and reducing teenage pregnancy.

The proposals, drawn up as part of a review of the U.K. broadcast advertising code, would ease long-standing restrictions that limited when condom commercials could be shown. Condom advertisements had traditionally been confined largely to late-evening slots, on the grounds that they dealt with sexual matters unsuitable for younger audiences.

Under the proposed rules, condom adverts would be permitted more broadly on television, though they would still be barred from programmes made for or primarily watched by young children. Regulators said the aim was to balance child-protection concerns with the need to provide clear sexual-health information to older teenagers and adults.

The move came amid continuing concern over Britain’s teenage pregnancy rate, which for years had been among the highest in Western Europe. Public health advocates argued that restricting condom advertising to late-night schedules undermined efforts to reach young people before they became sexually active or while they were forming attitudes toward contraception.

Baroness Joyce Gould, a Labour peer and prominent sexual-health campaigner, played a leading role in pressing for a more open approach. As chair of the Independent Advisory Group on Sexual Health and HIV, Gould argued that condom advertising should be treated as part of a wider public-health strategy rather than as a taboo subject. She and other campaigners said responsible advertising could help normalize condom use, reduce unintended pregnancies and limit the spread of sexually transmitted infections.

Supporters of the changes said teenagers were already exposed to sexual imagery in entertainment and online media, while receiving too little practical information about contraception. They argued that television advertising, if regulated and responsibly scheduled, could reinforce safer-sex messages and complement school-based sex education and National Health Service campaigns.

Opponents, including some family and religious groups, warned that earlier condom advertising could sexualize children or be seen as encouraging underage sex. Regulators responded that the proposals would keep protections around children’s programming and would require adverts to be socially responsible, non-explicit and not targeted at younger children.

The proposed changes formed part of a broader debate in Britain over how far advertising rules should support public-health goals. For sexual-health organisations, the condom-advertising reforms were viewed as a practical step toward lowering teenage pregnancy rates and improving awareness of contraception. For critics, they raised questions about the boundary between health education and inappropriate exposure of children to sexual material.
